concept.name: Closed-end fund
concept.definition: A closed-end investment company — one of the three basic types of investment company — that issues a fixed number of shares in a one-time public offering. The shares then trade on an exchange at market prices determined by supply and demand, which can be above (a premium) or below (a discount) the fund's net asset value.
concept.intuition: A closed-end fund is a sealed pool of money: after the initial offering, the only way in or out is to trade the fund's shares with other investors, so the share price can drift away from the value of what the fund holds.
concept.mechanics: The fund does not continuously issue or redeem shares, so the manager invests a stable pool of capital, often using leverage. Share price is set by the market, while NAV is set by the portfolio; the gap between them is the premium or discount. Many CEFs pay regular distributions that can include return of capital.
concept.failure_modes: Discounts can persist or widen for years, so buying at a discount is not a reliable source of return. Leverage amplifies losses and can force distribution cuts in rising-rate or falling-asset environments.
concept.misconceptions: That a CEF trading below NAV is automatically a bargain — discounts often reflect fees, leverage costs, tax structures, or governance. Also, investors generally cannot redeem CEF shares at NAV the way they can mutual fund shares.
concept.example: A CEF holds a bond portfolio worth $20 per share but its shares trade at $18 — a 10% discount — because investors demand a yield cushion against its leverage.
